y-m-23-01.title: Where did Jiho's solution go off track?
y-m-23-01.topic: Writing a repeating decimal as a fraction
y-m-23-01.goal: In a solution that writes a repeating decimal as a fraction, find the line where a value is dropped without any reason, check the error by converting the result back to the original number, and then fix it correctly.
y-m-23-01.material: Jiho tried to write x = 0.4555… (the first decimal place is 4, and from the second decimal place on, 5 repeats forever) as a fraction in lowest terms, and solved it as follows. The lines of the solution are numbered from line 1 to line 4. Read aloud, it is 'zero point four five five five …, with 5 repeating'.
y-m-23-01.thinking.0: Checking whether each line of the solution follows exactly from the line before
y-m-23-01.thinking.1: Checking the result by converting it back to the original condition
y-m-23-01.thinking.2: Fixing the error and comparing it with another solution
y-m-23-01.prereq.0: The meaning of terminating decimals and repeating decimals, and the repeating block (the part that repeats after the decimal point)
y-m-23-01.prereq.1: Multiplying both sides by the same number keeps an equation true (level of linear equations)
y-m-23-01.prereq.2: Subtracting decimals, and writing fractions in lowest terms
y-m-23-01.s.s1.prompt: Pick the one line in Jiho's solution whose reasoning is not correct. (Lines are counted from 1.)
y-m-23-01.s.s1.hint.0: Subtract the decimals in line 1 and line 2 yourself, and check exactly what digits are left after the decimal point.
y-m-23-01.s.s1.line.2: The decimal part .1 is small, so treat it as nothing: 99x = 45
y-m-23-01.s.s1.explain: Line 3 is the line that goes wrong. Up to line 2, the repeating parts after the decimal point cancel each other, so 99x = 45.1 comes out exactly. But in line 3, .1 was thrown away because it is small. In an equation, if you throw away even a small number, the equation no longer holds. So the 5/11 in line 4 is 0.4545…, which differs from the original number 0.4555… at the third decimal place. If you chose line 1 or line 2: the calculation of 100x and its decimal part is actually correct.
y-m-23-01.s.s2.prompt: When you doubt whether Jiho's answer 5/11 is correct, what is the fastest check you can do without looking at the solution again?
y-m-23-01.s.s2.hint.1: Divide 5 by 11 and carry the calculation to four decimal places.
y-m-23-01.s.s2.o.a: Change 99 to 100 and calculate again in the same way
y-m-23-01.s.s2.r.a: This is a way of changing numbers until it works out when the calculation does not match. If there is no reason for the change, you cannot know whether the answer is correct.
y-m-23-01.s.s2.o.b: The answer is a simple-looking fraction, so I take it to be correct
y-m-23-01.s.s2.r.b: A fraction being in a simple form is a separate matter from its value being correct. Even a fraction in lowest terms can be wrong.
y-m-23-01.s.s2.o.c: Write 5/11 as a decimal and compare it with 0.4555…
y-m-23-01.s.s2.r.c: You thought of checking by converting the answer back to the original number. It is a way of verifying with the result instead of trusting the solving process.
y-m-23-01.s.s2.explain: If you convert the answer back to a decimal, 5/11 = 0.4545…, which differs from 0.4555… at the third decimal place. If you compare the result with the original condition like this, you can tell there is an error without rereading the solution.
y-m-23-01.s.s3.prompt: Write how line 3 should be corrected, and then find the value of x as a fraction in lowest terms. If you solved it another way, you may use that method.
y-m-23-01.s.s3.hint.0: Keep the value that was thrown away in line 3, and rewrite what 99x equals.
y-m-23-01.s.s3.hint.1: Multiply both sides by the same number so that only whole numbers remain, and check whether the two numbers have a common divisor.
y-m-23-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you convert your fraction back to a decimal and check that it equals 0.4555…?
y-m-23-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you explain in your own words why the discarded value changes the result?
y-m-23-01.s.s3.selfAssess.2: If you solved it another way, did you compare whether the answers of the two methods are the same?
y-m-23-01.s.s3.model.0: In line 3 you must not throw away .1; you should keep 99x = 45.1. Multiplying both sides by 10 gives 990x = 451, and x = 451/990 = 41/90.
y-m-23-01.s.s3.model.1: 10x = 4.555… and 100x = 45.555…, so 100x − 10x = 41, 90x = 41, and x = 41/90. Without throwing away any decimal part, subtract two equations whose repeating parts are the same.
y-m-23-01.s.s3.modelNote.1: Another method: subtract equations that are set up so that the repeating parts are the same.

y-m-23-02.title: To know the 100th digit after the decimal point
y-m-23-02.topic: The nth decimal place of a repeating decimal
y-m-23-02.goal: Sort out what information is needed to know the digit at any place of a repeating decimal (where the repetition starts and what the repeating block is), and check how the position calculation changes when the start is not the first place.
y-m-23-02.material: When 5÷14 is written as a decimal, the digits after the decimal point, starting from the first decimal place, go 3, 5, 7, 1, 4, 2, 8, 5, 7, 1, 4, 2, 8, … You want to find the digit in the 100th decimal place. In this task, decimal places are always counted with 'the place right after the decimal point as the first place'. Since 5÷14 is less than 1, its whole-number part is 0.
y-m-23-02.thinking.0: Judging whether the information is enough
y-m-23-02.thinking.1: Finding the error in a solution that matches positions with the repeating block
y-m-23-02.thinking.2: Making several examples that satisfy a condition and explaining the rule
y-m-23-02.prereq.0: Division that writes a fraction as a decimal (to how many decimal places)
y-m-23-02.prereq.1: The meaning of the repeating block
y-m-23-02.prereq.2: The quotient and remainder of a division
y-m-23-02.s.s1.prompt: You divided 5÷14 with a calculator and got 0.3571428571… (shown to 10 decimal places), and you want to find the digit in the 100th decimal place. Besides these 10 digits, what more do you need to know to be sure of the 100th digit? Choose everything that is needed.
y-m-23-02.s.s1.hint.0: Number the 10 digits one by one, and mark where the same group of digits appears again.
y-m-23-02.s.s1.hint.1: Look at whether there are digits before the marked group that do not repeat.
y-m-23-02.s.s1.o.a: The fact that the numerator is 5
y-m-23-02.s.s1.r.a: You already know the value of the numerator. It is not new information, just a property of the number you already wrote.
y-m-23-02.s.s1.o.b: From which decimal place the decimal starts repeating
y-m-23-02.s.s1.r.b: You asked separately about the place where the repetition starts, so you are thinking about the front part and the repeating part separately.
y-m-23-02.s.s1.o.c: The sum of the first five digits after the decimal point
y-m-23-02.s.s1.r.c: The sum of the digits is of no use for deciding the position. What you need is which digit sits in which place.
y-m-23-02.s.s1.o.d: The repeating digits and their order
y-m-23-02.s.s1.r.d: You saw that you need to know the content of the repeating part to read off a digit from a position.
y-m-23-02.s.s1.explain: The 100th digit is determined only when you have both 'the repeating digits and their order' and 'from which decimal place the repetition starts'. Right now only 10 digits are shown, so you also need to check with the remainders of the division that the repetition really continues as 5, 7, 1, 4, 2, 8.
y-m-23-02.s.s2.prompt: When you checked by dividing, 571428 repeated forever starting from the second decimal place (the 3 in the first place does not repeat). Pick the one line in one student's solution whose reasoning is not correct. (Lines are counted from 1.)
y-m-23-02.s.s2.hint.0: Write the place number and the digit as pairs from the first decimal place to the thirteenth, and find the place number where the repeating block first appears.
y-m-23-02.s.s2.hint.1: Compare the place number where the first digit of the block, 5, sits with the place number where the second 5 sits.
y-m-23-02.s.s2.line.0: 5÷14 = 0.3571428571428…, and 571428 repeats from the second decimal place. The repeating block has 6 digits.
y-m-23-02.s.s2.line.1: To find the 100th place, find the remainder when 100 is divided by 6 and look it up in the block.
y-m-23-02.s.s2.line.2: Since 100 = 6 × 16 + 4, the 100th digit is the same as the 4th digit of the block.
y-m-23-02.s.s2.line.3: The 4th digit of 571428 is 4, so the 100th digit is 4.
y-m-23-02.s.s2.explain: Line 2 and line 3 are off. The block starts from the second decimal place, so the 100th place is the same as the (100 − 1)th place of the block, that is, the 99th place. Since 99 = 6 × 16 + 3, the answer is 1, the 3rd digit of the block. Line 1 correctly states where the repetition starts and the length of the block, and line 4 just follows the line before it.
y-m-23-02.s.s3.prompt: Find 3 different values of n for which the digit in the nth decimal place is 4. (n is a natural number from 1 to 100.)
y-m-23-02.s.s3.hint.0: Write the digits after the decimal point up to the 13th place and mark the place numbers where a 4 appears.
y-m-23-02.s.s3.hint.1: Compare the gaps between the marked place numbers.
y-m-23-02.s.s3.ok.c1: It is a natural number from 1 to 100.
y-m-23-02.s.s3.fail.c1: Please make n a natural number from 1 to 100.
y-m-23-02.s.s3.ok.c2: The digit in that place is 4.
y-m-23-02.s.s3.fail.c2: The digit in that place is not 4. Count the place numbers again to check.
y-m-23-02.s.s3.explain: The digit 4 first appears at the 5th place, and since the block length is 6, it appears again every 6 places. So 5, 11, 17, …, 95 are all possible (16 in all up to 100).
y-m-23-02.s.s3.because.prompt: Write the rule among the values of n you found, and also write how you can use this rule to find a larger n.
y-m-23-02.s.s3.because.hint.0: List the values of n you found from smallest to largest and find the difference between each pair of neighboring numbers.
y-m-23-02.s.s3.because.hint.1: Compare that difference with some value of the repeating block.
y-m-23-02.s.s3.because.selfAssess.0: Did you check that the values of n you found all have the same gap?
y-m-23-02.s.s3.because.selfAssess.1: Did you explain in your own words why the gap equals the block length?
y-m-23-02.s.s3.because.selfAssess.2: Did you pick one larger n found by the rule and check that it really works?
y-m-23-02.s.s3.because.model.0: They grow by 6 each time, like 5, 11, 17. The block has 6 digits, so the same digit comes back 6 places later; you just keep adding 6 to 5.
y-m-23-02.s.s3.because.model.1: The first place where 4 appears is the 5th, and after the block length of 6 the same digit appears again, so I can find 11, 17, 23, ….
y-m-23-02.s.s3.because.modelNote.1: An answer that explains the same rule as starting from 5 and adding gaps of 6, in a different way

y-m-23-03.title: What happens when you add two endless decimals?
y-m-23-03.goal: Show with a counterexample made by the student that the generalization 'adding repeating decimals gives a repeating decimal' does not hold, and rewrite the claim so that it is true.
y-m-23-03.material: Seoyun said, 'If you add two decimals that go on forever (repeating decimals), the sum is always a decimal that goes on forever too.' In this task, she decided to test it using only fractions a/12 with denominator 12 (a is a natural number from 1 to 11). Every fraction, when written as a decimal, is either a decimal that ends (a terminating decimal) or a decimal that goes on forever (a repeating decimal).
y-m-23-03.thinking.0: Choosing a way to test a claim that contains 'always'
y-m-23-03.thinking.1: Making several counterexamples that satisfy a condition yourself
y-m-23-03.thinking.2: Rewriting a false claim so that it becomes true
y-m-23-03.prereq.0: The meaning of terminating decimals and repeating decimals
y-m-23-03.prereq.1: How to write a fraction with denominator 12 as a decimal (division)
y-m-23-03.s.s1.prompt: Seoyun thinks, 'If you add two decimals that go on forever (repeating decimals), the sum is always a decimal that goes on forever too.' What is the most fitting attitude to take when you first meet this idea?
y-m-23-03.s.s1.o.a: It is right. If you add two numbers with no end, the sum will have no end either
y-m-23-03.s.s1.r.a: You looked only at the shape 'endless' and assumed the sum has the same shape. You can only know what the sum is by calculating.
y-m-23-03.s.s1.o.b: Because of 'always', it is worth looking for an example where the sum ends
y-m-23-03.s.s1.r.b: This is an attempt to find one example that breaks the word 'always'. It is a direction that tests the claim.
y-m-23-03.s.s1.o.c: I will not decide whether it is right or wrong before calculating a few examples
y-m-23-03.s.s1.r.c: This is a careful attitude that holds off on a conclusion until evidence has gathered.
y-m-23-03.s.s1.explain: A claim that contains 'always' can fall apart with a single counterexample. So looking for an example where the sum ends is a good start. Calculating first and then judging is also reasonable.
y-m-23-03.s.s1.acc.0: Deciding after calculating examples is also a reasonable start. But if you have the goal of finding an example that breaks 'always', you can test it faster.
y-m-23-03.s.s2.prompt: Choose two fractions a/12 and c/12 with denominator 12. (a and c are natural numbers from 1 to 11.) Make 3 different pairs where both fractions go on forever when written as decimals, and the sum of the two fractions ends when written as a decimal. Swapping only the order of the two numbers counts as the same pair.
y-m-23-03.s.s2.hint.0: Make a table of a/12 for a = 1, 2, 3, … written as decimals, showing whether each one ends or goes on forever.
y-m-23-03.s.s2.hint.1: Add two endless fractions and look at how the denominator and numerator change.
y-m-23-03.s.s2.var.a: a (the numerator of the first fraction)
y-m-23-03.s.s2.var.c: c (the numerator of the second fraction)
y-m-23-03.s.s2.ok.c1: a and c are natural numbers from 1 to 11.
y-m-23-03.s.s2.fail.c1: Please make a and c natural numbers from 1 to 11.
y-m-23-03.s.s2.ok.c2: a/12 is a decimal that goes on forever.
y-m-23-03.s.s2.fail.c2: a/12 is a number that ends when written as a decimal. Pick one that goes on forever.
y-m-23-03.s.s2.ok.c3: c/12 is a decimal that goes on forever.
y-m-23-03.s.s2.fail.c3: c/12 is a number that ends when written as a decimal. Pick one that goes on forever.
y-m-23-03.s.s2.ok.c4: The sum (a+c)/12 is a decimal that ends.
y-m-23-03.s.s2.fail.c4: The sum (a+c)/12 is still a decimal that goes on forever. Look for a pair whose sum ends.
y-m-23-03.s.s2.explain: For example, 1/12 = 0.0833… and 2/12 = 0.1666… go on forever, but their sum 3/12 = 1/4 = 0.25 ends. If the remainders of a and c when divided by 3 are different, so that the sum is a multiple of 3, it always works (a and c are both not multiples of 3 and a+c is a multiple of 3).
y-m-23-03.s.s3.prompt: Rewrite Seoyun's idea so that it is correct. Include one of the examples you just made as evidence.
y-m-23-03.s.s3.hint.0: Pick one pair you just made and write the two fractions and the sum as decimals side by side.
y-m-23-03.s.s3.hint.1: Think about what word you could put in place of 'always' in Seoyun's statement so that it is no longer false.
y-m-23-03.s.s3.selfAssess.0: In your example, did you check that both fractions really go on forever as decimals?
y-m-23-03.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you explain in your own words why your corrected sentence is not false?
y-m-23-03.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you also think about 'what condition is needed for the sum to end'?
y-m-23-03.s.s3.model.0: 'It always becomes a repeating decimal' is wrong. 1/12 = 0.0833… and 2/12 = 0.1666… go on forever, but their sum 3/12 = 0.25 ends. It should be corrected to 'the sum may be an endless decimal or it may end'.
y-m-23-03.s.s3.model.1: It is not always so. If you add 4/12 = 0.333… and 5/12 = 0.4166…, you get 9/12 = 0.75, which ends. So 'the sum can be a repeating decimal or a terminating decimal' is right.
y-m-23-03.s.s3.modelNote.1: It showed the same conclusion with another example.

y-m-23-04.topic: Comparing the sizes of repeating decimals
y-m-23-04.goal: When the first few places are the same, check when you can decide which of two repeating decimals is larger, by using the first place where they differ and a comparison of fractions, while revising your judgment and your confidence.
y-m-23-04.thinking.0: Holding off on a conclusion when information is lacking
y-m-23-04.thinking.1: Considering how new information affects your judgment and confidence
y-m-23-04.thinking.2: Checking the results of a decimal comparison and a fraction comparison against each other
y-m-23-04.prereq.0: The meaning of terminating decimals and repeating decimals
y-m-23-04.prereq.1: Comparing the sizes of decimals (comparing place by place)
y-m-23-04.prereq.2: Finding a common denominator and comparing fractions
y-m-23-04.s.s1.hint.0: Each time new information appears, compare whether your judgment became more certain, changed, or stayed the same.
y-m-23-04.s.s1.hint.1: Say out loud once, before you start, from which place you begin looking when comparing two decimals.
y-m-23-04.s.s1.st.0.ask: With only this information, what can you say about the sizes of A and B?
y-m-23-04.s.s1.st.0.after: You cannot say two numbers are equal just because they agree up to the second place. You need to find the first place where the digits differ.
y-m-23-04.s.s1.st.0.o.a: Both start with 0.45, so A and B are the same number
y-m-23-04.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You assumed that if the first few places are the same, the whole numbers are the same. You still do not know what the following digits are like.
y-m-23-04.s.s1.st.0.o.c: It is not yet decided which of A and B is bigger
y-m-23-04.s.s1.st.0.r.c: This is a judgment that held off on a conclusion after looking only up to the same place. You saw that you need to look at the next place.
y-m-23-04.s.s1.st.1.ask: How can you describe the sizes of A and B now?
y-m-23-04.s.s1.st.1.after: If you compare the digits at the first place where they differ, B looks bigger. If 9 kept going after that, they could become equal, like 0.4549999… = 0.455, so you can trust it more once you check that the repeating part is not 9.
y-m-23-04.s.s1.st.1.o.a: A is bigger. Because the later places change more
y-m-23-04.s.s1.st.1.r.a: Changing in many places and being larger are separate things. The digit at the first place that differs decides the size.
y-m-23-04.s.s1.st.1.o.b: B is bigger. They first differ at the third place, and B's digit is larger
y-m-23-04.s.s1.st.1.r.b: You are using the method of comparing the digits at the first place where they differ.
y-m-23-04.s.s1.st.1.o.c: I see B as bigger, but I will check the exception where everything after is 9
y-m-23-04.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You reach a conclusion but adjust your confidence by considering the possibility of an exception.
y-m-23-04.s.s1.st.2.info: Written as fractions, A = 5/11 and B = 41/90. With the least common multiple of the two denominators, 990, as the common denominator, A = 450/990 and B = 451/990.
y-m-23-04.s.s1.st.2.ask: How would you describe the sizes of the two numbers now?
y-m-23-04.s.s1.st.2.after: Comparing as fractions, it is certain that B > A. It is the same as the conclusion from comparing decimal places. It was right that they differ at the third place.
y-m-23-04.s.s1.st.2.o.a: B is bigger than A. The difference is 1/990, which is very small
y-m-23-04.s.s1.st.2.r.a: You made the two fractions have the same denominator and compared the numerators. Even a small difference does not change the size relationship.
y-m-23-04.s.s1.st.2.o.b: The difference between A and B is very small, so it is fine to regard them as the same number
y-m-23-04.s.s1.st.2.r.b: You did not distinguish between 'almost the same' and 'the same'. If there is a difference, they are different numbers.
y-m-23-04.s.s1.st.2.o.c: A is bigger. The fraction with the smaller denominator is the bigger number
y-m-23-04.s.s1.st.2.r.c: You looked only at the denominator without looking at the numerator and denominator together. If the numerators are different, you cannot compare by the denominators alone.
y-m-23-04.s.s1.reflect: At first, 'not yet decided' was the most reasonable. Looking at the place where they first differ, the third place, supports the judgment that B is bigger, and converting to fractions makes it certain. What matters is that you did not say the numbers are the same just because the first few places are the same.
y-m-23-04.s.s2.prompt: In two sentences or fewer, write what you learned in this activity about 'the point at which you can decide the sizes of two decimals'.
y-m-23-04.s.s2.hint.0: Compare the first piece of information revealed with the last, and find what changed.
y-m-23-04.s.s2.hint.1: Pick just one piece of information that changed your judgment.
y-m-23-04.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Can you say at which of the three steps of this activity you got what you wrote?
y-m-23-04.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you set a numerical rule in advance like 'it is enough if the first few places are the same'?
y-m-23-04.s.s2.selfAssess.2: If you know the exception (like 0.4999…), did you include it?
y-m-23-04.s.s2.model.0: Even if they agree up to the second place, they are not the same number. You just find the first place where the digits differ and compare them, and this time it was the third place.
y-m-23-04.s.s2.model.1: Knowing only how many places are the same is not enough; comparing the digit at the first place that differs, or converting to fractions to check, makes it certain. But there is an exception when 9 keeps going, like 0.4999….
y-m-23-04.s.s2.modelNote.1: An answer that also mentions the exception

y-m-23-05.title: If the denominator is big, is the repeating block long too?
y-m-23-05.topic: The length of the repeating block and remainders
y-m-23-05.goal: Evaluate 'the bigger the denominator, the longer the block' with a counterexample from a table, and explain with the number of possible remainders that the block length has a limit, while distinguishing the limit from the actual length.
y-m-23-05.material:
Minseo said, 'The bigger the denominator of a fraction, the longer the block becomes when it is written as a decimal.' Below is a table of four fractions with numerator 1 written as decimals. The length of the block is the number of digits that repeat.
Fraction / Decimal / Block / Block length
1/3 / 0.333… / 3 / 1
1/7 / 0.142857142857… / 142857 / 6
1/11 / 0.090909… / 09 / 2
1/13 / 0.076923076923… / 076923 / 6
(A block can also start with 0. Example: the block of 1/13 is 076923)
y-m-23-05.thinking.0: Telling apart the examples that fit a claim from the ones that do not
y-m-23-05.thinking.1: Finding the error in the evidence within a solution
y-m-23-05.thinking.2: Explaining the difference between a limit (maximum) and an actual value
y-m-23-05.prereq.0: Division and remainders when writing a fraction as a decimal
y-m-23-05.prereq.1: The meaning of the repeating block
y-m-23-05.s.s1.prompt: Look at the table and evaluate Minseo's claim 'the bigger the denominator, the longer the block'. Which is the most fitting?
y-m-23-05.s.s1.o.a: For 1/7 and 1/11, the one with the bigger denominator has the shorter block, so the claim is wrong
y-m-23-05.s.s1.r.a: You found a pair where the one with the bigger denominator has the shorter block. You used an example that breaks the claim as your evidence.
y-m-23-05.s.s1.o.b: When the denominator went from 3 to 7 the block got longer, so the claim is right
y-m-23-05.s.s1.r.b: You collected only examples where the claim holds. 'The bigger' talks about all cases, so you must also check whether any example does not fit.
y-m-23-05.s.s1.o.c: There are only four examples, so I think this table cannot tell whether it is right or wrong
y-m-23-05.s.s1.r.c: You held off on every conclusion because there are few examples. But to show that a claim is wrong, a single example is enough.
y-m-23-05.s.s1.explain: 'The bigger, the longer' is a claim about all cases. Comparing 1/7 (block of 6 digits) and 1/11 (block of 2 digits), the block of 1/11, which has the bigger denominator, is shorter, so it breaks the claim. Even with many examples, collecting only the ones that fit does not make a claim true, but one wrong example is enough.
y-m-23-05.s.s2.prompt: Minseo explained with remainders 'how long the block of 1/7 can be'. Pick the one line whose reasoning is not correct. (Lines are counted from 1.)
y-m-23-05.s.s2.hint.0: Apply what line 3 says to the list in line 2, and rewrite what remains in the list.
y-m-23-05.s.s2.line.0: If you divide 1 by 7 and keep calculating after the decimal point, a remainder appears each time.
y-m-23-05.s.s2.line.1: The possible values of the remainder are the 7 values 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.
y-m-23-05.s.s2.line.2: If the remainder becomes 0, the division comes out even and the decimal ends, but 1/7 does not end, so 0 does not appear.
y-m-23-05.s.s2.line.3: If the same remainder appears again, the same digits repeat from there on.
y-m-23-05.s.s2.line.4: Therefore the block of 1/7 can be at most 7 digits long.
y-m-23-05.s.s2.explain: Line 5 is off. Line 3 said 0 does not appear, so the remainders are only the 6 values 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. Since there are 6 possible remainders before the same remainder repeats, the block is at most 6 digits. Line 2 lists all the possible values, and it is in line 3 that the list must be reduced.
y-m-23-05.s.s3.prompt: Write how many digits the block of 1/13, whose denominator is 13, can have at most, with the reason. In the table the block of 1/13 has 6 digits; also write in one sentence how this relates to 'at most'.
y-m-23-05.s.s3.hint.0: Change the explanation for 1/7 to the denominator 13 and list the possible remainders yourself.
y-m-23-05.s.s3.hint.1: Compare which is larger: the 6 digits in the table or the number you just counted.
y-m-23-05.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you explain in your own words why 0 is left out of the possible remainder values?
y-m-23-05.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you explain, using the example in the table, that 'at most' does not mean it always reaches that much?
y-m-23-05.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you distinguish between 'the larger the denominator, the larger the maximum length can be' and 'it is actually long'?
y-m-23-05.s.s3.model.0: Only the 12 remainders from 1 to 12 are possible (because if it becomes 0, it ends). When the same remainder appears, it repeats, so the block is at most 12 digits. In fact it is 6 digits, so the maximum is just a limit that cannot be exceeded, not something that is always reached.
y-m-23-05.s.s3.model.1: If you leave out 0, there are 12 possible remainders, so it cannot exceed 12 digits. 1/13 having 6 digits means it did not use up the limit.
y-m-23-05.s.s3.modelNote.1: An answer that distinguishes the limit from the actual length

y-m-23-06.title: Designing a repeating decimal with denominator 11
y-m-23-06.topic: The denominator when a repeating decimal is written as a fraction
y-m-23-06.goal: Design several repeating decimals with a two-digit block whose fraction in lowest terms has denominator 11, find what the numbers you made have in common, and test that common feature with a new number.
y-m-23-06.material: 0.abab… is a number in which the first decimal digit a and the second decimal digit b repeat. For example, if a = 1 and b = 2, it is 0.1212… (12 repeating forever). a and b are single digits from 0 to 9, and a may be 0 (example: 0.0909…). Read aloud, it is 'zero point a b a b…'.
y-m-23-06.thinking.0: Designing a number that satisfies a condition yourself
y-m-23-06.thinking.1: Finding a common rule among several solutions
y-m-23-06.thinking.2: Testing the rule you found with a new example
y-m-23-06.prereq.0: How to write a repeating decimal as a fraction
y-m-23-06.prereq.1: Fractions in lowest terms and the greatest common divisor
y-m-23-06.s.s1.prompt: When 0.1212… (12 repeating forever) and 0.0909… (09 repeating forever) are written as fractions and then reduced to lowest terms, what is each denominator?
y-m-23-06.s.s1.hint.0: Write each number as a fraction, and check whether there is a number that divides both the numerator and the denominator.
y-m-23-06.s.s1.hint.1: If there is such a number, divide and then compare the denominators.
y-m-23-06.s.s1.o.a: Even after reducing both to lowest terms, the denominator stays 99
y-m-23-06.s.s1.r.a: You wrote them with 99 but did not check whether they can be reduced further. If the numerator and 99 have a common divisor, the denominator of the fraction in lowest terms changes.
y-m-23-06.s.s1.r.b: You reduced the denominator 99 together with the numerator and noticed that the denominators become different for each.
y-m-23-06.s.s1.o.c: Both can be written as fractions with denominator 100
y-m-23-06.s.s1.r.c: You thought of a repeating decimal as a fraction with denominator 100. A decimal that goes on forever cannot be written with 100.
y-m-23-06.s.s1.explain: 0.1212… = 12/99 = 4/33 and 0.0909… = 9/99 = 1/11. Even for repeating decimals of the same form, the denominator of the fraction in lowest terms differs depending on the digits of the block.
y-m-23-06.s.s2.prompt: Make the number 0.abab… in which the two digits 'ab' repeat forever from the first decimal place. (Example: if a = 1 and b = 2, 0.1212…) a and b are single digits from 0 to 9. Make 3 different numbers whose denominator is 11 when written as a fraction in lowest terms.
y-m-23-06.s.s2.hint.0: Make a few, like 0.0909… and 0.1818…, write them as fractions, and compare the denominators.
y-m-23-06.s.s2.hint.1: Organize in a table whether the two digits a and b of the numbers with denominator 11 have a common relationship.
y-m-23-06.s.s2.ok.c1: a and b are single digits from 0 to 9.
y-m-23-06.s.s2.fail.c1: Please make a and b single digits from 0 to 9.
y-m-23-06.s.s2.ok.c2: The denominator of the fraction in lowest terms is 11.
y-m-23-06.s.s2.fail.c2: The denominator is not 11 when written as a fraction in lowest terms. Convert it to a fraction and check.
y-m-23-06.s.s2.explain: 0.0909… = 1/11, 0.1818… = 2/11, 0.2727… = 3/11, and so on all have denominator 11. There are 10 possibilities (a, b) = (0, 9), (1, 8), (2, 7), …, (9, 0) (the sum is 9). 0.9999…, which is 99/99, has denominator 1, so it does not work.
y-m-23-06.s.s2.because.prompt: Write what a and b have in common in the numbers you made, and also write one way to check that this common feature holds in every case.
y-m-23-06.s.s2.because.hint.0: Write the a and b of each number you made as a pair, and try adding or subtracting them.
y-m-23-06.s.s2.because.hint.1: Pick one number you have not made yet and test whether the common feature you found holds.
y-m-23-06.s.s2.because.placeholder: Example: if a and b are …, then …
y-m-23-06.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you check one by one that the common feature you found fits all the numbers you made?
y-m-23-06.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you try to explain in your own words why the common feature is related to the denominator 11?
y-m-23-06.s.s2.because.selfAssess.2: Did you check that there is no number that fits the common feature but whose denominator is not 11?
y-m-23-06.s.s2.because.model.0: Adding a and b always gives 9. 0.0909…, 0.1818…, and 0.2727… are like that. If I convert 0.3636…, which I have not made yet, to a fraction, it is 36/99 = 4/11, so it fits.
y-m-23-06.s.s2.because.model.1: The two-digit number ab is always a multiple of 9 (09, 18, 27). For a new one, I can convert 0.4545… directly to a fraction and check whether it becomes 5/11.
y-m-23-06.s.s2.because.modelNote.1: An answer that states multiples of 9 and uses direct checking as the method

y-m-23-07.title: Is the decimal on the calculator screen 1/7?
y-m-23-07.topic: Judging whether a decimal repeats from what is shown on the screen
y-m-23-07.goal: Understand that a decimal of which only a finite number of places is visible cannot settle whether it repeats or what the fraction's value is, and tell apart information that is enough to settle it from information that only raises confidence.
y-m-23-07.material: A calculator shows only up to 12 decimal places and throws away the rest (for example, 0.1428571428571… is shown as 0.142857142857). You calculated some number N (the value of a fraction p/q made of natural numbers p and q) and the screen showed 0.142857142857. 1/7 is a number like 0.142857142857142857… in which 142857 repeats forever. Read aloud, it is 'zero point one four two eight five seven one four two eight five seven'.
y-m-23-07.thinking.0: Distinguishing the places that are visible from the ones that are not
y-m-23-07.thinking.1: Distinguishing enough information from insufficient information
y-m-23-07.thinking.2: Adjusting your judgment and confidence according to the information
y-m-23-07.prereq.1: Division that writes a fraction as a decimal
y-m-23-07.s.s1.prompt: You calculated a number N with a calculator and got 0.142857142857. This calculator shows only up to 12 decimal places and throws away the rest. The digits on the screen look like 142857 repeated twice. Can you settle that N is 1/7?
y-m-23-07.s.s1.hint.0: Separate the 12 places you can see on the screen from the places you cannot see.
y-m-23-07.s.s1.hint.1: Try to make up one example of two different numbers that look the same up to 12 places.
y-m-23-07.s.s1.o.a: It cannot be settled from the screen alone. It could differ in places outside the screen
y-m-23-07.s.s1.r.a: You pointed out that there are places you cannot see. You saw that there is no guarantee the pattern in the visible places continues.
y-m-23-07.s.s1.o.b: It is probably 1/7, but I will not settle on it before checking more
y-m-23-07.s.s1.r.b: This is a judgment that sees it as likely but holds off on settling it. You distinguished confidence from certainty.
y-m-23-07.s.s1.o.c: It can be settled. 142857 repeated twice, so it will keep repeating
y-m-23-07.s.s1.r.c: You thought that two repetitions will continue from now on. A few visible repetitions can give confidence but are not a guarantee.
y-m-23-07.s.s1.explain: The screen shows only 12 places, so you cannot know how things continue from the 13th place on. For example, N could be a fraction with a very large denominator, and a different digit could come after 142857142857…. 'It is very likely 1/7' and 'it can be settled' are different things.
y-m-23-07.s.s1.acc.0: 'It is probably 1/7' is a reasonable expectation, and it is valid because you did not settle on it. But in the next step, think about what information would let you settle it.
y-m-23-07.s.s2.prompt: Which of the following would be enough to settle that N is 1/7? Choose everything that is enough. (You may choose every option that is enough on its own.)
y-m-23-07.s.s2.hint.0: Calculate one example of how close two fractions with small denominators can be to each other.
y-m-23-07.s.s2.hint.1: Think about what must happen to the denominator if two numbers that are the same up to 12 places are different fractions.
y-m-23-07.s.s2.o.a: The result from another calculator that shows the same repetition up to 100 decimal places
y-m-23-07.s.s2.r.a: When more places are visible, confidence grows. But places that cannot be seen still remain, so it is not enough to settle it.
y-m-23-07.s.s2.o.b: The expression (the values of the numerator and denominator) that was entered into the calculator to get N
y-m-23-07.s.s2.r.b: You saw that if you know where the calculation came from, you can check the value directly. It is an approach that does not depend on the screen.
y-m-23-07.s.s2.o.c: The fact that the digit in the first place on the screen is 1
y-m-23-07.s.s2.r.c: This is a fact already visible on the screen. It is not new information, so it cannot change your judgment.
y-m-23-07.s.s2.o.d: The fact that N is a fraction of natural numbers with denominator 1000 or less
y-m-23-07.s.s2.r.d: You recalled that if the denominator has a limit, there are not many different fractions with similar values.
y-m-23-07.s.s2.explain: If you know the expression that was entered, you can check the value directly. Also, if you know that N is a fraction with denominator at most 1000, two different such fractions cannot look the same up to 12 places, so you can settle that N = 1/7. Showing 100 more places only raises confidence and does not guarantee anything.
y-m-23-07.s.s2.acc.0: If you know the expression, you can calculate and check the value of N directly, so it is enough.
y-m-23-07.s.s2.acc.1: The difference between two different fractions with denominators at most 1000 cannot be smaller than 1/(1000×1000), so if they agree up to 12 places they are the same number. So this alone is enough.
y-m-23-07.s.s3.prompt: Compare your first judgment on 'Is N equal to 1/7?' with your judgment now. Include how your judgment changes depending on what information you have.
y-m-23-07.s.s3.hint.0: Write your first judgment and the newly learned information side by side, one line each.
y-m-23-07.s.s3.hint.1: Write separately what the conclusion is when you do not have the information and when you do.
y-m-23-07.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you write 'confidence is high' and 'it can be settled' as different things?
y-m-23-07.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you write the needed information specifically (the limit on the denominator, the expression, and so on)?
y-m-23-07.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you write the conclusion without the information and the conclusion with the information separately?
y-m-23-07.s.s3.model.0: With only the 12 places on the screen, you cannot settle that it is 1/7. But if you know that N is a fraction with denominator at most 1000, you can settle that it is 1/7.
y-m-23-07.s.s3.model.1: It is probably 1/7, but I did not settle on it because the later digits could differ. If I know the expression that was entered or check directly that the remainders repeat, I can settle it.
y-m-23-07.s.s3.modelNote.1: An answer that distinguishes confidence from certainty

y-m-23-08.title: Making decimals whose repetition starts late
y-m-23-08.goal: Tell apart the fractions that, when written as decimals, have a front part that ends and a back part that repeats, and design several such fractions yourself to find what their denominators have in common.
y-m-23-08.material: When fractions are written as decimals, some repeat from the first decimal place, like 1/3 = 0.333…; some, like 1/6 = 0.1666…, have a 1 in the first place that is not part of the repetition and 6 repeats from the second place on. There are also decimals that end, like 1/4 = 0.25. In this task, you only deal with fractions a/b where a < b ≤ 60.
y-m-23-08.thinking.0: Guessing the relationship between the structure of a fraction's denominator and the shape of its decimal
y-m-23-08.thinking.1: Making fractions that satisfy a condition yourself
y-m-23-08.thinking.2: Finding what the examples you made have in common and guessing why
y-m-23-08.prereq.0: Division that writes a fraction as a decimal
y-m-23-08.prereq.1: The meaning of terminating decimals and repeating decimals
y-m-23-08.prereq.2: Fractions in lowest terms and common divisors
y-m-23-08.s.s1.prompt: When fractions are written as decimals, which ones start repeating not at the first decimal place but after it? (Ones like 1/6 = 0.1666…, where one or two digits at the front are not part of the repetition.) Choose all of them.
y-m-23-08.s.s1.hint.0: Work out each fraction by division to four decimal places.
y-m-23-08.s.s1.hint.1: Looking at the four decimal places, mark where the repetition begins.
y-m-23-08.s.s1.r.a: You thought of 0.1666…. The first place is 1, and 6 repeats from the second place.
y-m-23-08.s.s1.r.b: You thought of 0.111…. The repetition starts right from the first place.
y-m-23-08.s.s1.r.c: You thought of 0.05. This decimal ends and does not repeat.
y-m-23-08.s.s1.r.d: You thought of 0.08333…. 3 repeats from the third place.
y-m-23-08.s.s1.r.e: You thought of 0.142857…. 142857 repeats from the first place.
y-m-23-08.s.s1.explain: 1/6 = 0.1666… and 1/12 = 0.08333… have places at the front that are not part of the repetition. 1/9 and 1/7 repeat right from the first place, and 1/20 = 0.05 is a decimal that ends.
y-m-23-08.s.s2.prompt: Make 3 different fractions a/b (a and b are natural numbers, a < b ≤ 60) that go on forever when written as decimals and whose repetition starts after the first decimal place, not at it. (Fractions with the same value count as the same one. Example: 1/6 and 2/12 are the same.)
y-m-23-08.s.s2.hint.0: Write each fraction as a decimal one at a time and collect in a table where the repetition starts.
y-m-23-08.s.s2.hint.1: Divide them into two groups, those whose repetition starts right away and those whose repetition starts late, and compare the denominators.
y-m-23-08.s.s2.ok.c1: a is a natural number that is at least 1 and a < b ≤ 60.
y-m-23-08.s.s2.fail.c1: Please make a and b natural numbers with a < b ≤ 60.
y-m-23-08.s.s2.ok.c2: It goes on forever when written as a decimal.
y-m-23-08.s.s2.fail.c2: It is a number that ends when written as a decimal. Pick a fraction that goes on forever.
y-m-23-08.s.s2.ok.c3: The repetition starts after the first place, not at it.
y-m-23-08.s.s2.fail.c3: The repetition starts right from the first decimal place. Look for a number that has places at the front that are not part of the repetition.
y-m-23-08.s.s2.explain: 1/6 = 0.1666…, 1/12 = 0.08333…, 1/15 = 0.0666…, 7/30 = 0.2333…, and 1/14 = 0.0714285714285… all have places at the front that are not part of the repetition. Every case where, in lowest terms, the denominator has 2 or 5 and also has a prime factor other than 2 and 5 fits.
y-m-23-08.s.s2.because.prompt: Write what the denominators (in lowest terms) of the fractions you made have in common, and guess and write why such fractions start repeating late.
y-m-23-08.s.s2.because.hint.0: Reduce the fractions you made to lowest terms and list their denominators together.
y-m-23-08.s.s2.because.hint.1: Put them next to the denominators of the fractions whose repetition starts right away and find the difference.
y-m-23-08.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Do you see the same common feature in all the fractions you made?
y-m-23-08.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you compare with the denominators of the fractions whose repetition starts right away?
y-m-23-08.s.s2.because.selfAssess.2: Is your guess about 'why' connected to evidence (for example, the denominator condition for terminating decimals)?
y-m-23-08.s.s2.because.model.0: The denominator has 2 or 5 in it and also another number such as 3. 6, 12, 15, and 30 are all like that. If there are only 2s and 5s it ends, and if there are only 3s it repeats right away, so when the two kinds are mixed, the front ends and the back repeats, it seems.
y-m-23-08.s.s2.because.model.1: Like 6, 14, 15, they are multiples of 2 or 5 and also multiples of 3 or 7. The two kinds are mixed, so the front part ends and the back part repeats.
y-m-23-08.s.s2.because.modelNote.1: An answer that also includes a denominator containing 7
